lessons.title: Knowing and Understanding the Past
lessons.notes_html:
What Is History?

History is the study of the past. It gives us information about people, historical events and places of old times.

How Do We Study History?

We study history through two kinds of sources:

  • Primary sources — things and accounts from the time itself, such as old objects, buildings and eyewitness accounts.
  • Secondary sources — books and writings prepared later from the primary sources.

It is essential that history is based on evidence and logical ideas, so that it is fully authentic (true and trustworthy).

Why Is History Important?

  • Knowing the past helps us understand the present and prepare for the future.
  • We learn lessons from past events and can stop them from happening again.
  • Knowing the history of our country and nation creates a feeling of identity and pride in us.
  • It helps us play our part for the betterment of our country.

Writing the History of Your Own Area

To find the history of the area where you live, ask your parents and the elders who have lived there for a long time. Find out: how old the area is, which are its old families, what work its people do, what their beliefs and laws were, and which things they used in daily life.

Facts and Views

When many people tell the story of the same event, some details are the same in every story — these are facts. Some details are different — these are each person's own views. A true history is written by selecting only the facts and the things proven by evidence.

mcqs.why: The book explains that things which are the same in everyone's story are facts, while different details are each person's own views. A complete history is written using only the facts.

lessons.title: The Beginning of Human Life
lessons.notes_html:
Two Theories About the Beginning of Human Life

  • Theory of Creation: Allah created man from clay and made him His vicegerent (khalifa) on earth. Man is the offspring of Hazrat Adam (AS).
  • Theory of Evolution: Human life began from simple life. It kept changing over millions of years through natural selection, and humans were born from chimpanzee-like ancestors.

Scientists think that humans appeared from their chimpanzee-like ancestors about six million years ago. Modern humans are called Homo Sapiens.

Important Words

  • Bipedal means the ability to walk on two feet.
  • Early humans wandered from place to place in search of food.

Early Humans and Modern Humans

PointEarly HumansModern Humans
HomeLived in jungles and caves; no permanent homeLive in cities and houses
FoodHunted animals; ate wild fruits and rootsObtain food through agriculture and trade
ToolsUsed stone toolsUse modern tools and machines
Other pointsCovered their bodies with animal skinsHave education, writing and technology

Life of Hunter-Gatherer Bands

  • They lived in jungles in small bands (groups) and had no permanent home.
  • They hunted animals and ate fruits and roots of trees.
  • They used stone tools and moved from place to place in search of food.
  • They lived in caves and covered their bodies with animal skins.

Benefits of their lifestyle: a simple life close to nature, few belongings and few worries, and working together in a group. Harms: danger of food shortage, no permanent home or protection, and danger from disease and wild animals.

Today's lifestyle — benefits: availability of food, water and treatment; education and technology; safe and permanent homes. Harms: environmental pollution, less physical labour and new diseases, greater expense and busyness.

mcqs.why: The book names two theories: the theory of creation and the theory of evolution. The first says Allah created man from clay; the second says life changed over millions of years by natural selection.

mcqs.why: The theory of creation says Allah created man from clay and made him His vicegerent on earth. Man is the offspring of Hazrat Adam (AS).

mcqs.why: The theory of evolution says human life began from simple life and, changing through natural selection over millions of years, humans were born from chimpanzee-like ancestors.

mcqs.q: Scientists think humans appeared from their ancestors about ____ million years ago.
mcqs.why: The book says scientists think humans were born from their chimpanzee-like ancestors about six million years ago. This long period shows change happened very slowly.

mcqs.q: Modern humans are called ____.
mcqs.why: The scientific name of modern humans given in the book is Homo Sapiens. Early humans were different in lifestyle, tools and homes.

mcqs.q: Bipedal means ____.
options: the ability to walk on two feet
mcqs.why: Bipedal means the ability to walk on two feet. This was an important feature in the development of human beings.

mcqs.q: Early humans wandered from place to place in search of ____.
mcqs.why: The book says early humans wandered from place to place in search of food. They had no permanent home because they depended on hunting and wild fruits.

mcqs.q: What did hunter-gatherer bands use as tools?
mcqs.why: Early humans and hunter-gatherer bands used stone tools for hunting and cutting. Metal tools and machines came much later in human history.

mcqs.q: Which is a harm (disadvantage) of the hunter-gatherer lifestyle?
mcqs.why: The book lists danger of food shortage, no permanent home and danger from disease and wild animals as harms of that lifestyle. A simple life and group work were its benefits.

mcqs.q: How do modern humans obtain their food?
mcqs.why: The comparison table in the book says modern humans obtain food through agriculture and trade, while early humans hunted and ate wild fruits and roots.

lessons.title: Society
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Society?

Society is a group of people who live together with a feeling of togetherness and mutual relation. They cooperate with one another, and their beliefs, standards, customs and values are shared.

Culture is the lifestyle of a group of people. It includes the language of common conversation, religion, food and drink, dress habits, music and art, and the things passed from one generation to another.

When Did Society Begin?

Society came into existence about one hundred thousand years ago. An agricultural society is one in which crops are cultivated and animals are reared. The change from an agricultural society to an industrial society took place in the late eighteenth century (about 1769, after the Industrial Revolution). Today's society can be called a post-industrial society.

Hunter-Gatherer Bands and Agricultural Society

PointHunter-Gatherer BandsAgricultural Society
Sources of foodHunting, wild fruits and rootsCultivation of crops and rearing animals
Division of workNo special division; all joined in searching for foodWork divided — some cultivated, some reared animals, some made pots and tools
PopulationSmall groups, low populationPopulation grew; villages and towns formed
MovementKept moving in search of foodSettled permanently in one place
Clothes and shelterAnimal skins, caves, temporary shelterCloth and permanent houses
Relation with natureComplete dependence on natureEffort to control nature (cultivation, irrigation)
BenefitsSimple lifeAbundance of food and permanent residence
HarmsDanger of food shortageMore labour and dependence on land

How Societies Organise, Survive and Continue

For their organisation, survival and continuity, societies make laws and customs, divide work, cooperate with one another, pass their culture and values to the next generation through education and training, and arrange protection and food for their members.

Why Do Societies Change?

  • New technology and inventions, e.g. the discovery of agriculture and the Industrial Revolution.
  • Change in the natural environment, e.g. weather or the changing course of rivers.
  • Trade and contact with other societies.

Why Do Societies Remain (Stay the Same)?

  • Shared culture, traditions and beliefs.
  • Laws and organisation which keep the society established.
  • Values passed from one generation to another through education.

Examples from Pakistan: more population in cities because there are more job opportunities; schools and hospitals increasing in villages due to the attention of government and people; use of mobiles and internet increased because of new technology. Things that have not changed: the basis of religion and beliefs, the tradition of family and hospitality, celebrating Eids and festivals, and attachment to our own language and dress.

mcqs.q: Society came into existence about ____ thousand years ago.
mcqs.why: The book says society came into existence about one hundred thousand years ago. After that, human groups slowly developed into different kinds of societies.

mcqs.q: An agricultural society is one in which crops are cultivated and animals are ____.
mcqs.why: The book defines an agricultural society as one in which crops are cultivated and animals are reared. This settled way of getting food replaced hunting and gathering.

mcqs.q: The change from an agricultural society to an industrial society took place in ____.
mcqs.why: The book says this change took place in the late eighteenth century, about 1769, after the Industrial Revolution, when machines and factories began.

mcqs.q: Today's society can be called a ____ society.
mcqs.why: The book says today's society can be called a post-industrial society, in which most people are busy in providing information and services rather than making goods.

mcqs.q: Culture includes all of the following EXCEPT ____.
mcqs.why: Culture is the lifestyle of a group: language, religion, food and drink, dress, music and art, and things passed from generation to generation. The course of rivers is part of nature, not culture.

mcqs.q: In an agricultural society, what happened to the population?
options: It grew and villages and towns formed
mcqs.why: The comparison table says that in an agricultural society the population grew and villages and towns formed, because people settled permanently in one place with enough food.

mcqs.q: How was work divided in an agricultural society?
options: Some cultivated, some reared animals, some made pots and tools
mcqs.why: The book says work was divided in an agricultural society: some people cultivated crops, some reared animals and some made pots and tools. Hunter-gatherer bands had no such special division.

mcqs.q: Which is a reason why societies change?
mcqs.why: Societies change because of new technology and inventions, changes in the natural environment, and trade and contact with other societies. Shared traditions and beliefs are reasons why societies remain the same.

mcqs.q: Why is there more population in Pakistani cities, according to the book's example?
mcqs.why: The book gives this example of change in Pakistani society: there is more population in cities because there are more job opportunities in cities.

mcqs.q: Which of these has NOT changed in our society?
options: The tradition of family and hospitality
mcqs.why: The book lists the tradition of family and hospitality, the basis of religion and beliefs, celebrating Eids and festivals, and attachment to language and dress as things in which no change has come.

mcqs.q: For their survival and continuity, societies pass their culture and values to the next generation through ____.
mcqs.why: The book says societies make laws and customs, divide work, cooperate, arrange food and protection, and pass culture and values to the next generation through education and training.

mcqs.q: In hunter-gatherer bands, clothes and shelter were ____.
options: animal skins, caves and temporary shelter
mcqs.why: The comparison table says hunter-gatherers wore animal skins and lived in caves and temporary shelters, while agricultural people used cloth and permanent houses.

lessons.title: The Beginning of Civilization
lessons.notes_html:
Worldview

The collection of beliefs about life and the world is called a worldview. A person's personal worldview is affected by: characteristics received in inheritance, life experiences (of home, school and community), the environment and culture in which we live, and family and school.

When most members of a society share the same beliefs about life and the world, it is called a social worldview. For example, the people of the Indus Valley Civilization gave great importance to cleanliness, so their cities had an excellent system of brick drains and bathrooms — that was their shared worldview.

What Is a Civilization?

A society which attains the highest quality of social development and organisation is called a civilization.

Characteristics of a Civilization (with Pakistan's examples)

CharacteristicExample from Pakistan
Large urban centresKarachi, Lahore, Islamabad
Specialisation of workFarmers, labourers, doctors, teachers, engineers
Social classesDifferent professions and classes
Balanced food supplyAbundance of food from agriculture
ReligionIslam and other religions
Central governmentFederal and provincial government
WritingUrdu and English writing
Art and architectureBadshahi Mosque, Mazar-e-Quaid, folk art
Technology and inventionsMobile phones, internet, machines

Development, Technology and the Environment

With social development and technology, facilities of treatment, clean water, better food and education increase, which improves health and prosperity; but more machines and pollution also create new diseases. We obtain harmony with the environment by wearing clothes according to the weather, building houses, using fans, heaters and roofs, and using river and rain water for cultivation and drinking.

The standard of our life is guaranteed by our society, government, family and ourselves. For future generations we give education to children, keep the environment clean, plant trees, save water and resources, and carry forward good laws and customs.

mcqs.q: The collection of beliefs about life and the world is called ____.
mcqs.why: The book defines worldview as the collection of beliefs about life and the world. When most members of a society share these beliefs, it becomes a social worldview.

mcqs.q: When most members of a society share beliefs about life and the world, it means there is a ____.
mcqs.why: The book says that when most members of a society share beliefs about life and the world, it means a social worldview. The Indus Valley people's love of cleanliness is its example.

mcqs.q: A society which attains the highest quality of social development and organisation is called a ____.
mcqs.why: This is the book's definition of civilization. Such a society has large cities, specialisation of work, writing, government, art and technology.

mcqs.q: Which of these affects a person's personal worldview?
options: Life experiences of home, school and community
mcqs.why: The book lists inheritance, life experiences of home, school and community, the environment and culture, and family and school as the things that shape a person's personal worldview.

mcqs.q: The excellent brick drains and bathrooms of Indus Valley cities show that its people gave great importance to ____.
mcqs.why: The book explains the social worldview with this example: the Indus Valley people valued cleanliness, so their cities had an excellent system of brick drains and bathrooms.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of a civilization?
mcqs.why: The nine characteristics listed in the book include large urban centres, specialisation of work, social classes, balanced food supply, religion, central government, writing, art and architecture, and technology.

mcqs.q: In the Pakistan example, Badshahi Mosque and Mazar-e-Quaid show the characteristic of ____.
mcqs.why: In the book's table of Pakistan's civilization, Badshahi Mosque, Mazar-e-Quaid and folk art are given as examples of art and architecture.

mcqs.q: How does social development and technology improve health?
options: By increasing facilities of treatment, clean water, better food and education
mcqs.why: The book says development and technology increase treatment facilities, clean water, better food and education, which improves health and prosperity — though pollution from machines also creates new diseases.

mcqs.q: Which is one way we obtain harmony with the environment?
options: Wearing clothes according to the weather and building houses
mcqs.why: The book says we wear clothes according to the weather, build houses, use fans, heaters and roofs, and use river and rain water for cultivation and drinking to live in harmony with the environment.

mcqs.q: For future generations, we ensure the standard of life by ____.
options: giving education to children, keeping the environment clean and planting trees
mcqs.why: The book says we give education to children, keep the environment clean, plant trees, save water and resources from being wasted, and carry forward good laws and customs for future generations.

lessons.title: Unit 1 — End Exercises
lessons.notes_html:
Matching: Types of Societies

SocietyStatement
AgriculturalPeople settled in one place for obtaining food and rearing animals
Hunter-gatherer bandsPeople kept moving from one place to another in search of food
Pastoralism (herdsmen)People kept migrating so that their animals could get food
IndustrialPeople use raw materials for the production of things
Post-industrialPeople were mostly busy in providing information

Three Sources of Historical Evidence

  1. Observations — eyewitness accounts.
  2. Archaeological remains — things found by digging.
  3. Written records — written documents.

Characteristics of Civilization in the Indus Valley

  • Large urban centres — Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro.
  • Specialisation of work — farmers, craftsmen, traders.
  • Balanced food supply — abundance of food from agriculture and trade.
  • Central government — planned cities and rules.
  • Writing — pictorial symbols on seals.
  • Art and architecture — houses of baked bricks, the Great Bath, statues, jewellery.
  • Technology — the system of measurement, metal-working, bull carts and boats.

Life of the Early Humans

Early humans lived in jungles and caves and had no permanent home. They hunted and ate the meat of animals and the fruits and roots of trees. They used stone tools, moved from place to place in search of food, and covered their bodies with animal skins.

Work of a Historian

A historian researches past events, people and places, collects evidence and writes history. His responsibilities include studying archaeological remains and documents, examining evidence, and writing reports and books. The qualities he needs most are truthfulness, examination of evidence, patience and interest in research. His interesting work is discovering the secrets of old civilizations and bringing the stories of the past to light.

If There Were No History

Without knowledge of the past we would not understand the present, we would repeat the mistakes of the past, we would lose our identity and pride, and we could not prepare for the future. History teaches us not to repeat past mistakes, gives us our identity, and helps us understand the present and prepare for the future.

people using raw materials in factories

mcqs.why: The end exercises explain the three sources: observations are eyewitness accounts, archaeological remains are things found by digging, and written records are written documents.

mcqs.why: The book says all characteristics of civilization are found in the Indus Valley; Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro are its large urban centres. Its writing is seen in the pictorial symbols on seals.

mcqs.why: Houses of baked bricks, the Great Bath, statues and jewellery are listed under art and architecture of the Indus Valley Civilization. Farmers, craftsmen and traders show specialisation of work.

mcqs.why: The end exercises state that the Indus Valley's writing appears as pictorial symbols on seals. Its technology included measurement systems, metal-working, bull carts and boats.

mcqs.why: The description of early humans' life says they lived in jungles and caves, used stone tools and covered their bodies with animal skins. Cloth came later, with settled societies.

mcqs.why: The end exercises explain that with the discovery of agriculture, hunter-gatherer bands changed into an agricultural society, and with the Industrial Revolution the agricultural society changed into an industrial society.

mcqs.why: The discussion points say the most important characteristics for a historian's work are truthfulness, examination of evidence, patience and interest in research.

mcqs.q: If there were no information related to history, we would ____.

people moving in search of food
mcqs.why: Agricultural society is matched with people settled in one place for obtaining food and rearing animals. Moving in search of food describes hunter-gatherer bands.

mcqs.why: The book lists planned cities and rules as the sign of a central government in the Indus Valley Civilization. A central government organises the cities and enforces rules.

lessons.title: Land and People of the Indus Valley Civilization
lessons.notes_html:
Where and When?

The Indus Valley Civilization flourished in Asia (South Asia), on the bank of the River Indus. It remained continuously from about 3300 to 1300 years ago, so it belongs to the Bronze Age.

Two Central Cities

CityLocation
HarappaIn Punjab, on the bank of the River Ravi
Mohenjo-DaroIn Sindh, on the bank of the River Indus

How Do We Know About It?

Our information about its inhabitants and their ways has been obtained from the study of archaeological remains (artefacts found by digging) — buildings, seals, pots, statues, toys and other things. Their writing has not yet been read, so these remains are the important source of our information.

Famous Artefacts and Their Meanings

ArtefactDetail
Dancing GirlA statue of copper made in a special style
SealsSquare pieces of engraved stones which traders used in business
BowlRound and deep, used for eating
BullA very tall horned animal engraved on seals
DiceColoured cube with a different number of holes on each side

Children's toys included small carts with clay wheels, dice and figures of different animals.

Sanitary System

Dirty water from houses went through drains into the drains of the streets and from there out of the city. Houses had bathrooms and wells, and the streets had brick drains joined to the drains of the houses.

Professions of the People

Farming, rearing animals, making pots, making cloth, making jewellery, trade and labour.

A House of Mohenjo-Daro

Walls of baked bricks, a central courtyard, rooms around it, a well, a bathroom and drains.

mcqs.q: The Indus Valley Civilization flourished on the bank of the ____.
mcqs.why: The book says the Indus Valley Civilization flourished in Asia (South Asia) along the River Indus. Harappa was on the Ravi, but the civilization as a whole grew along the Indus.

mcqs.q: The Indus Valley Civilization remained continuously from about ____ to ____ years ago.
mcqs.why: The book gives its period as about 3300 to 1300 years ago. It is therefore also called a civilization of the Bronze Age.

mcqs.q: The two central cities of the Indus Valley Civilization were ____.
mcqs.why: Harappa (in Punjab, on the River Ravi) and Mohenjo-Daro (in Sindh, on the River Indus) were the two central cities of this civilization.

mcqs.q: Mohenjo-Daro is located in ____, on the bank of the River Indus.
mcqs.why: The book says Mohenjo-Daro is in Sindh on the bank of the River Indus, while Harappa is in Punjab on the bank of the River Ravi.

mcqs.q: Our information about the Indus Valley people has been obtained from the study of ____.
mcqs.why: Their writing has not yet been read, so archaeological remains — buildings, seals, pots, statues and toys found by digging — are the important source of information about them.

mcqs.q: In the matching exercise, 'Seals' are described as ____.
options: square pieces of engraved stones used by traders in business
mcqs.why: The book matches seals with square pieces of engraved stones which traders used in business. The coloured cube with holes is the dice, and the copper statue is the Dancing Girl.

mcqs.q: Children's toys in the Indus Valley included ____.
options: small carts with clay wheels and dice
mcqs.why: The book says children's toys included small carts with clay wheels, dice and figures of different animals, all made of clay and simple materials.

mcqs.q: How did dirty water leave the houses in Indus Valley cities?
options: It was thrown in the streets
Through drains into street drains and then out of the city
mcqs.why: The sanitary system was excellent: dirty water from houses went through drains into the street drains and from there out of the city. Houses also had bathrooms and wells.

mcqs.q: To which age does the Indus Valley Civilization belong?
mcqs.why: The book places the civilization, about 3300 to 1300 years ago, in the Bronze Age, when bronze tools were in use.

mcqs.q: Which of these was a profession of the Indus Valley inhabitants?
mcqs.why: Their professions were farming, rearing animals, making pots, making cloth, making jewellery, trade and labour. Machines and printing came thousands of years later.

lessons.title: Art and Architecture of the Indus Valley Civilization
lessons.notes_html:
Experts in Town Planning and Architecture

The inhabitants of the Indus Valley Civilization were experts in town planning and architecture. Their houses and buildings were made of baked bricks.

Town Planning

  • Cities were built in a grid pattern — straight streets from north to south and from east to west.
  • The city was divided into several blocks; wide streets could let two bull carts pass together.
  • Houses were built on both sides of the streets, and drains were built along them.
  • The ratio of bricks was kept at 1:2:4.

The Houses

  • Wide walls of baked bricks; a central courtyard with rooms around it.
  • Some houses were even two or three storeys high.
  • Houses had a well, a bathroom and a drainage system; stairs were built for going to the roof.

Kinds of Art

Three samples of art found here are stone carving, pottery (pots) and jewellery-making. The full list of their arts: stone carving, pottery, jewellery-making, dance and music, and writing.

ArtefactArt it shows
Upper torso of the priestStone carving
Figures of a dancing girlDance
Stringed instrumentsMusic
Bowl made of baked clayPottery
Seal with pictorial symbolsWriting

The statue of a dancing girl shows the people were fond of dance. Written seals were used for trade — this shows that the traders here could write.

mcqs.q: The inhabitants of the Indus Valley Civilization were experts in town planning and ____.
mcqs.why: The book says they were experts in town planning and architecture. Their planned cities, straight streets and brick houses prove this skill.

mcqs.q: The houses and other buildings of the Indus Valley were made of ____.
mcqs.why: The book says houses and buildings were made of baked bricks, with the brick ratio kept at 1:2:4. Baked bricks made the buildings strong and lasting.

mcqs.q: Cities were built in a grid pattern, which means ____.
options: straight streets from north to south and east to west
mcqs.why: Town planning in the Indus Valley used a grid pattern: straight streets running north–south and east–west, with the city divided into blocks and houses on both sides.

mcqs.q: The ratio of bricks used in the buildings was kept at ____.
mcqs.why: The book says the ratio of bricks was kept at 1:2:4 in the Indus Valley buildings. This fixed ratio shows their advanced building science.

mcqs.q: Houses of the Indus Valley had a central ____ with rooms around it.
mcqs.why: The book describes houses with a central courtyard and rooms around it, a well, a bathroom, drains and stairs to the roof. Some houses were two or three storeys high.

mcqs.q: The statue found from the Indus Valley which shows the people's love of dance is the statue of ____.
mcqs.why: The book says we know the inhabitants were fond of dance because a statue of a dancing girl has been found there. It is a famous copper statue made in a special style.

mcqs.q: Written seals used for trade show that the traders of the Indus Valley could ____.
mcqs.why: The book says written seals were used for trade, which shows that the traders could write. The seals carried pictorial symbols.

Things of other countries were found in Indus Valley cities — for example seals of Mesopotamia, minerals of Afghanistan and Iran, copper of India and green carnelian of China — and things of the Indus Valley (seals, beads) were found in other countries.

lessons.notes_html:
When Did It End?

The Indus Valley Civilization came to an end in about 1300 years ago (about 1300 BCE in the book's counting of 'years ago' from its period 3300–1300). Historians have still not been able to discover the certain reasons which caused the decline (end) of the civilization.

Three Viewpoints About the End

ViewpointArgument given for it
Aryan invasion — the Aryans invaded and destroyed the civilizationThe Vedic hymns mention the destruction of cities; human skeletons were found in Mohenjo-Daro
Floods — floods forced people to leave their homesFloods came in the River Indus; the city had to be rebuilt
Climate change — change in the monsoon and rise in temperature caused droughtAgriculture and trade depended on rain; people moved to other places

Importance of the Indus Valley Civilization

  • Town planning and architecture — planned cities with straight streets and baked-brick houses.
  • Cleanliness — an excellent system of brick drains and bathrooms.
  • Peace and tranquillity — it was a powerful civilization living in peace.
  • Various kinds of art and handicraft samples which are still common today.

Its people did not leave big monuments like the people of Egypt and Mesopotamia, but the remains of their cities are still visible today, and even today the people of Pakistan and India use many of their things.

Two Lessons for Our Cities Today

  • An excellent system of cleanliness and water drainage — brick drains in houses and streets, and arrangement for collecting rubbish.
  • Town planning — straight streets, a city divided into blocks, and access of clean water to every house.

Elements Still Present in Pakistan and India Today

Houses of baked bricks and houses with courtyards; wells and bathrooms; brick drains and the water drainage system; clay pots; beads and jewellery; bull carts; weaving and sewing of cloth; dice and toys; weights and balances in trade.

  • Food: then too they ate grain, fruit and meat; today too the same food is eaten.

lessons.title: Government
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Government?

The system under which a community governs is called government. Government is a group of people which exercises its powers in a country (state). It has the authority to make laws and public policies for the whole country in order to rule the country.

System of Government in Pakistan

In Pakistan there is a federal, parliamentary and democratic system of government.

Purposes of Government

  1. To protect the lives and property of the citizens.
  2. To protect the fundamental rights of the people — these rights are recorded in Pakistan's Constitution of 1973.
  3. To provide public services for the betterment of the people, such as education and health services.
  4. To protect the ideology and identity of the country.
  5. To make trade agreements with other states for the protection of national interests.

Federal System

In a federal government, powers are divided between the federal (national) government and the provincial governments. Each level has full powers in several matters, while some powers are shared. The federal government deals with matters affecting the whole country — defence, foreign affairs and finance — while provincial governments deal with matters such as education and health. Both levels have the power to levy taxes.

Federal Units of Pakistan

  • The four provinces: Sindh, Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan.
  • The Federal Capital Territory: Islamabad.
  • Gilgit-Baltistan.

Parliamentary System

The important characteristic of the parliamentary system is that the legislature and the executive are not separate — the powers of the executive are not separated from the legislature. The Prime Minister selects the executive; the cabinet consists of members of the legislature under the Prime Minister's leadership, and the executive is answerable to the law-making assembly.

Democratic System

In a democratic government, people elect their representatives through elections. Not everyone can govern himself, so all adult citizens take part in free, fair and regularly held elections and choose their representatives by voting.

Checking the Government

We check how far the government has succeeded by judging it against its own purposes: Were lives and property protected? Were fundamental rights protected? Were public services like education and health received? Was the ideology and identity of the country protected? Were national interests protected?

lessons.title: Structure and Functions of the Federal Government
lessons.notes_html:
Three Branches of Government

The three branches of government are the legislature (law-making), the executive and the judiciary.

1. The Legislature (Parliament)

Parliament consists of two houses: the National Assembly (lower house) and the Senate (upper house). Duties of the law-making branch:

  • Legislation — making new laws and improving existing laws; laws are debated before approval.
  • Representation — members are the representatives of the people and keep contact between the people and the government.
  • Checking and supervision — the assemblies supervise the executive through oral and written questions to ministers, so that it remains answerable.
  • Selection and training — assemblies select and train future leaders.
  • Answerability — assemblies review the work of the government.

The Senate is a permanent law-making institution which guarantees continuity in national affairs, represents equality among the provinces and promotes harmony. It has 104 members; the term of its members is six years, and elections for half of its members are held again after three years.

The National Assembly has 342 members in total: 272 are elected for a term of five years, and the remaining 70 (60 women and 10 non-Muslims) are elected in proportion to the seats won by the political parties. On election day people vote in their constituency; the candidate receiving the most votes becomes a member (MNA).

2. The Executive

The executive enforces the law and runs the government. It includes the President and the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is the head of the government; the President is the head of the state. The Prime Minister forms the executive: the cabinet's ministers are selected from among the members of the National Assembly to run the different ministries. Duties: ensuring enforcement of the law, implementing policies, running the day-to-day work of government, maintaining law and order, and taking emergency action in emergency situations.

3. The Judiciary

The judiciary provides justice and interprets the law. It includes the Supreme Court (the highest court of Pakistan), the High Courts, the Federal Shariat Court and the subordinate courts. Its importance: it protects and defends the Constitution, decides disputes between the federal and provincial governments, hears appeals against decisions of subordinate courts, can take suo motu action in important matters, reviews the laws passed by Parliament, and protects the fundamental rights of citizens. The decision of the Supreme Court is binding on the federal and provincial governments.

Federal and Provincial Governments: Similarity and Difference

PointFederalProvincial
SimilarityBoth are organised in the same three branches — legislature, executive and judiciary — with the same kinds of duties
LegislatureTwo houses: National Assembly and SenateOne house: Provincial Assembly
Executive headsPresident and Prime MinisterGovernor (head of province) and Chief Minister (head of provincial government)
Biggest courtSupreme CourtHigh Court (subordinate courts work under it)

Five Very Important Rights (from the chapter)

Protection of life and property; protection of fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and access to information; receiving public services such as education and health; equality before the law — the law is supreme and all citizens are equal in its eyes; and the democratic right to vote in free, fair and regular elections.

lessons.title: Local Government
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Local Government?

Local government is the lowest level of government. It runs the administration of a single district, tehsil and union council. It is formed of the elected representatives of the people and gives people the right and authority to decide in matters affecting them.

Structure: A Three-Tier System

Under the Sindh Local Government Act 2013, local government has three tiers. Each tier is run by elected Chairmen and Vice-Chairmen; in big cities the heads are called Mayor and Deputy Mayor.

TierLevelHead
Union CouncilThe basic tier, consisting of villagesElected Chairman and Vice-Chairman
Tehsil CouncilThe tehsil levelElected Chairman and Vice-Chairman
District CouncilThe district levelElected Chairman and Vice-Chairman
Urban systemMetropolitan Corporation, Municipal Corporation, Town Committee, Union CommitteeIn big cities: Mayor and Deputy Mayor

Elections for the general seats of Union Councils are direct, while elections for the reserved seats of women, farmers, labourers and minorities are indirect. The Chairmen of the Union Councils serve for a term of four years.

Powers of the Union Council

  • Registering the births, deaths and marriages of children.
  • Repairing inns, drains and small roads.
  • Managing the cleaning of drains and toilets.
  • Working in agriculture, industry, trade, workshops, education and other matters.

Powers of the Tehsil Council

  • Approving development projects and the annual budget.
  • Providing, supervising and managing services.
  • Informing the district about the performance of government offices located in the tehsil.

Role and Duties of Local Government

Its purposes: to transfer powers to the lower level so that people's problems are solved; to give people opportunities to decide in matters affecting their lives; to let the local population allocate resources for necessary development; and to provide a strong foundation for practising democracy. Its duties include preparing annual development plans and budgets, collecting taxes, and providing public services such as cleaning of cities, repair, public parks, schools, hospitals, supply of drinking water and electricity.

Important Facts

  • In Pakistan, general elections are held after every five years.
  • The age of a voter is 18 years — every Pakistani citizen above eighteen years whose name is in the voters' list is eligible to vote.
  • The minimum age of a representative is 25 years (thirty years or more for the Senate).
  • The institution responsible for holding elections is the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP).

Meanings of the Terms

  • Election: the process under which the people of a constituency use their vote and elect their representatives.
  • Constituency: the area all of whose citizens have the right to vote at a specific time and whose people elect their representative.
  • Representative: the person elected for the law-making assembly; representatives make laws and decide the affairs of the state on behalf of the people.

Role of Different Groups in Elections

GroupRole
Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP)An independent institution (one Chief Election Commissioner and four members) which holds clean, transparent and fair elections; announces and conducts elections; prepares a correct voters' list; delimits constituencies; encourages voters; works on electoral reforms
Political partiesHelp voters get identity cards and enter their names in the electoral rolls; provide candidates and the party manifesto; inform people of the party's stance and promise to act on the manifesto; persuade people to vote for their candidate; appoint agents at polling stations
MediaBroadcasts pictures and news of all parties and candidates in an informed and impartial manner; asks candidates difficult questions about public problems; holds debates between candidates; publishes election results immediately
CitizensVote in local, provincial and national elections; may become a party member or a candidate; help the campaign with financial support; help voters come out on election day; play the role of an observer

How Citizens Can Improve Their Society

  • Stay informed about their village, town or city through newspapers, radio, television and the internet.
  • Write a letter to their MNA / MPA.
  • Take membership of a Community Based Organisation (CBO).
  • Keep their community clean and green, and obey the law.
  • Sign a memorandum; express views through peaceful demonstrations, sit-ins and boycotts.
  • Serve the country by joining the military or other institutions.

A Class Election

To elect a class monitor: nominate three candidates; each prepares a manifesto (what he or she will do for the pupils); candidates run their campaign and ask for votes; then voting is held, votes are counted and the winner is announced — candidate, manifesto, campaign, vote, counting and result, exactly as in real elections.

lessons.title: Media — Understanding and Role
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Media?

The different means (channels) of communicating with others are called media. Media are those means of communication through which news, information, entertainment, education and valuable messages are spread; they are called the means of mass communication. Examples: newspapers, TV, radio, journals, billboards, film, phone and the internet.

Four Forms of Media

FormMeaningExamples
Print mediaInformation transferred in paper form; communication through paper or hard clothNewspapers, journals, books
Electronic mediaThe use of electric means for contact with othersTelevision, radio
Digital mediaMedia understood through numerical signals by means of a machine (a message read through a signalling machine); can be seen, made, stored and improved on computersWebsites, email, the internet
Social mediaContact between people through internet and telephone technology; users exchange information, ideas, pictures and videosWhatsApp, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Google, YouTube

Roles of the Media

  1. News and information — conveys news about events in our country and around us; keeps us informed of social, political and economic affairs; warns about coming natural disasters so we can take precautions.
  2. Education — educational programmes give children the alphabet, numbers and knowledge of the world; programmes on science, technology, literature and politics educate adults; the internet plays a direct educational role.
  3. Increase in awareness — the most important role of the media: increasing people's awareness about social, political and economic affairs.
  4. Entertainment — audio (radio), visual (TV, cinema) and print media (journals, newspapers, books, cartoons).
  5. Public announcements — companies and institutions convey messages to the public, e.g. a warning about the spread of an epidemic, or information about elections.
  6. Advertisements — media advertises goods and services; advertisements encourage consumers to buy goods.
  7. Expression of opinion — people can now write letters to the editor, take part in discussions on radio and television, and comment online.

How the Internet Plays the Role of Media

The internet is a part of digital media, and social media also runs through it. It provides people of every age the opportunity to learn by themselves about different topics, and through it information, ideas, pictures and videos are promoted and exchanged.

lessons.title: Media in a Democratic Society
lessons.notes_html:
Why Media Matters in a Democracy

Democracy demands that citizens have the right to freedom of expression and access to information. The media helps in protecting and promoting these rights. It plays an important role in establishing a healthy democratic state: it keeps people informed of the work of public office-holders, keeps an eye on their performance, helps people make correct and responsible decisions in elections, brings transparency in public affairs, and gives the government an opportunity to reform.

The Media as a Guardian (Watchdog)

When the media reports about some action of public office-holders, it is playing the role of a guardian (watchdog). Access to information helps citizens make correct decisions about the personalities holding public offices.

What the Constitution Says

  • Article 19: every citizen shall have the right to freedom of speech and expression, and the media shall be free.
  • Article 19(A): every citizen shall have the right to access to information in all matters of public importance, keeping in view the reasonable restrictions imposed by law.

The media strengthens these rights because it provides information to citizens, keeps them informed of the performance of office-holders, gives people the opportunity to express their opinion, and makes office-holders answerable.

Media Should Be Free and Impartial

If the media has to play a correct role, it should be free and impartial — free from the control of the government — so that it can expose corruption and motivate the administration to take steps. Its freedom should be protected through laws so that, free from fear of punishment and harm, it can work openly for public rights.

Reasonable Restrictions on Freedom of Expression

According to Article 19, reasonable restrictions can be imposed by law with reference to: the glory of Islam; the security of Pakistan or any part of it; defence; friendly relations with foreign states; public order; decency and morality; contempt of court; and incitement to commit an offence.

PEMRA

In 2002 the Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) was created to run the electronic media in Pakistan according to regulations. Its duties are: (1) to raise the standard of information, awareness and entertainment; (2) to increase opportunities for choice of news, latest conditions, science and technology, music, sports and drama; (3) access of communication to the local community; (4) to ensure accountability, transparency and better governance through the provision of free information.

lessons.title: Demands of Media
lessons.notes_html:
Fact and Opinion

Sometimes the media does not only give information, but gives us an opinion (its own point of view). A fact can be proved — facts can be seen and tested directly. It is necessary to distinguish between fact and opinion because information provided by the media can be incomplete and misleading. Instead of immediately accepting information, we should first investigate and research, and then decide according to our own thinking.

Bias (Partiality)

The tendency to give preference to a person, group or point of view over another is called bias. Forms of bias in the media:

  • Deliberate mistake — presenting only one party's point of view, without the views of all sections of society.
  • Selection of the event — broadcasting the report of the same event repeatedly.
  • Choice of source — taking information only from sources which hold the same point of view.
  • Name-calling — using good words for one party and bad words for the other.
  • Placement of events — giving a prominent place to one event and keeping the other behind.
  • Length or depth — giving much time to one news item and very little to another.
  • Urban bias — giving priority to the news of cities over the news of villages.

Stereotyping

Stereotyping is a general characteristic which is presented with exaggeration about a group and applied to all the members of that group — seeing all members of a group in the same way. When all men or women are shown behaving in the same manner, it is an example of stereotyping. The chapter's examples of gender stereotyping: "Women look after the house" (women's work is only the house and children); "Men run the house" (only men earn and go out); the division of work between men and women is fixed.

Propaganda

A systematic effort made to promote one's own ideology or point of view is called propaganda. Its purpose is to influence the attitudes of people and to harm some other ideology or point of view. Through distorted and biased information, people form a wrong opinion without research and make wrong decisions.

Techniques of Propaganda

TechniqueMeaning
Card stackingBringing forward already selected points so that the biggest fault of the other side is highlighted
Name-callingLowering someone's reputation by using negative words
BandwagonPhrases such as "everyone is like this" or "everyone does this"
Arousing emotionsUsing information to arouse emotions (the technique of using information to arouse emotions is propaganda's emotional technique)
TransferAttributing the status or dignity of one thing to another so it appears dignified, or the fault of one thing to another so it is shown as bad
Glittering generalityPresenting a personality in an extremely positive way
TestimonialPraising an idea with reference to a well-known and famous personality
Plain folksBringing forward an ordinary personality so that ordinary people can be reached and their views supported

Advertisements and Bias

The important purpose of advertising is to persuade people to buy goods; for this, only the good aspect is highlighted in the advertisement. To test bias in an advertisement, check: has only one aspect been shown? Has one party been declared good and the other bad? Is the information incomplete or misleading? A suitable and balanced advertisement gives complete and unbiased information.

lessons.notes_html:
Matching: Terms and Definitions

TermDefinition
Bias (partiality)Giving preference to a person, group or point of view over others, even in a wrong way
FactAn event which has happened and which can be tested
MediaThe means of communication by which news, information, entertainment and education are spread
PropagandaSpreading opinions and ideas through organised efforts
Social mediaCommunication through social contacts

Role of the Media in Society

Conveying news and information; giving education; increasing awareness; providing entertainment; making public announcements; giving advertisements; giving the opportunity to express opinions. The most important role is to increase the awareness of the people.

Media and the Rights of Citizens

Article 19 of the Constitution gives every citizen the right to freedom of speech and expression, and the media is free; Article 19(A) gives every citizen the right of access to matters of public importance. The media encourages these rights: it provides information to citizens, keeps them informed of the performance of public office-holders, gives people the opportunity to express their opinion, and makes the office-holders answerable.

How Media Gives Incomplete and Misleading Information

  • Bias — presenting the point of view of one party only: selection of the event, choice of source, name-calling, placement of events, length or depth.
  • Stereotyping — presenting all the members of a group in the same way.
  • Propaganda — strengthening a particular way of thinking through distorted and biased information, using techniques like card stacking, name-calling, bandwagon, arousing emotions, transfer, glittering generality, testimonial and plain folks.

Awareness of these methods is necessary so that people do not form a wrong opinion without research and do not make wrong decisions; before accepting information, investigation and research should be done.

Writing a Good Report and Advertisement

A school-event report should keep a distinction between fact (the event which happened and can be tested) and opinion, and the information should be complete and unbiased. An advertisement's purpose is to persuade people to buy goods, but its information should be correct and complete — not only the good aspects — so bias is avoided.

lessons.title: The South Asia Region
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Region?

A region is a piece of land which has common characteristics — common physical characteristics (such as mountains, forests, wildlife and climate) or common human characteristics (such as language and form of government).

The Eight Countries of South Asia

Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.

Why Is South Asia a Separate Region?

  • Land: mountain ranges in the north, north-west and north-east surround it; the Arabian Sea lies in the south (to the south of Pakistan lies the Arabian Sea); India is a large peninsula.
  • Common physical characteristics: mountains, plains and climate.
  • Common history: except Afghanistan, Nepal and Bhutan, all countries remained under British rule until 1947.
  • Common characteristics of the inhabitants — common physical, human and historical characteristics.

Pakistan and India Compared

PointPakistanIndia
LandformsMountains in the north, plains, Arabian SeaHimalayas, Deccan Plateau, plains
InhabitantsMajority MuslimMulti-religious
ClimateHot and dryMonsoon climate
HistoryUnder British rule until 1947Under British rule until 1947

The similarities of the region are: common physical characteristics, common history (British rule until 1947) and common culture.

lessons.title: The Land of South Asia
lessons.notes_html:
How Mountains Are Formed

  • Fold mountains: when plates move towards each other and collide, the layers of rock meet and bend upwards and downwards, forming fold mountains. When mountain ranges change through upfolds and downfolds, fold mountains are formed.
  • Dome (uplifted) mountains: when plates move away from each other, cracks appear in the earth and magma (melted rock) rises up, pushing a part of the land upwards and forming a dome-shaped mountain.
  • Volcanic mountains: magma below the earth heats up and comes up, erupts from the top and spreads as lava (liquid matter); the lava cools and hardens and forms a cone-shaped volcanic mountain.

Main Landforms of South Asia

LandformDefinitionExamples from South Asia
MountainA high part of the land, much higher than the surrounding landHimalaya, Karakoram, Hindu Kush ranges
PlateauHigh and flat landDeccan Plateau (India), Pothohar (Pakistan), Balochistan Plateau
Plain regionLow and flat land formed from the fertile soil brought by riversIndus, Ganga and Brahmaputra plains

How Plains Are Formed

Plains are formed by erosion or deposition. Today's plains were once mountain ranges, valleys or underwater sea areas. (1) Erosion — mountains wear down through wind, water and ice. (2) Deposition — valleys and underwater sea areas fill up with the fertile soil brought by rivers and become plains.

The Three Large Plains of South Asia

The Indus plain (Pakistan), the Ganga plain (India) and the Brahmaputra plain (Bangladesh). The plains of the Indus (Mehran) and Ganga are so fertile because they are formed from the fertile soil (silt) brought by the rivers; every year floods and river water bring new fertile soil, which keeps the land fertile.

Why Do Most People Live in Plains?

Plain regions are flat and fertile; farming, water, transport, business, schools and hospitals are easily available there. In mountain regions, transport and farming are difficult.

Life in the Mountains

Animals found in the mountains of South Asia include the snow leopard, bear and markhor; plants include deodar, pine and fir.

mcqs.q: When plates move towards each other and collide, the layers of rock bend upwards and downwards and ____ mountains are formed.
mcqs.why: The book says that when plates move towards each other and collide, the rock layers meet and bend upwards and downwards (upfolds and downfolds), forming fold mountains.

mcqs.q: Dome-shaped mountains are formed when ____.
options: magma rises and pushes a part of the land upwards
mcqs.why: Dome (uplifted) mountains form when plates move away from each other, cracks appear, and magma rises up, pushing a part of the land upwards into a dome shape.

mcqs.q: When lava spreads on the surface of the earth, a cone-shaped mountain is formed which is called a ____ mountain.
mcqs.why: A volcanic mountain is cone-shaped: magma erupts from the top, spreads as lava, and the lava cools and hardens to form the cone.

mcqs.q: Plains are formed by erosion or ____.
mcqs.why: The book says plains are formed by erosion (mountains wearing down by wind, water and ice) or deposition (valleys and sea areas filling with fertile soil brought by rivers).

mcqs.why: The three large plains are the Indus (Pakistan), Ganga (India) and Brahmaputra (Bangladesh) plains, all formed from fertile river soil.

mcqs.why: A plateau is high and flat land; examples in South Asia are the Deccan Plateau (India), Pothohar (Pakistan) and the Balochistan Plateau. A plain is low and flat land.

mcqs.why: The landform table gives the Himalaya, Karakoram and Hindu Kush ranges as mountain examples from South Asia. The Deccan is a plateau and the Indus and Ganga are plains.

options: Because rivers bring new fertile soil (silt) every year
mcqs.why: The book says these plains are formed from the fertile soil brought by the rivers; every year floods and river water bring new fertile soil, which keeps the land fertile.

mcqs.q: Why do most people live in plain regions?
options: Because farming, water, transport, business, schools and hospitals are easily available there
mcqs.why: Plains are flat and fertile, so farming, water, transport, business, schools and hospitals are easily available. In mountain regions, transport and farming are difficult.

mcqs.why: The research activity names the snow leopard, bear and markhor as animals of the South Asian mountains, and deodar, pine and fir as their plants.

lessons.title: The People of South Asia
lessons.notes_html:
Facts About the Countries

  • The people of Nepal are called Nepali.
  • The two ethnic groups of Sri Lanka are Sinhalese and Tamil.
  • The majority of the people of Pakistan are Muslim.
  • Maldives consists of groups of islands; eighty percent of its people are associated with the profession of fishing.

Similarities and Differences

PointPakistanIndia
Ethnic groupsPunjabi, Sindhi, Pashtun, Baloch, etc.Many ethnic groups
ReligionIslam (majority)Hinduism, Islam, Sikhism, Christianity, etc.
FoodBread, rice, lentilsRice, bread, lentils
DressShalwar qameez, sariSari, dhoti, shalwar qameez
WorkAgriculture, industry, jobsAgriculture, industry, jobs

Similarities among the people of South Asia: common history and similar foods and dress. Differences: religion, language and ethnic groups.

Lifestyle of the People

Most people live in villages and practise agriculture; some live in cities and do jobs or business. Foods (bread, rice, lentils), dress (shalwar qameez, sari) and religious customs differ between countries, but the common history and culture bring the people close to one another.

Pakistan and Bangladesh Compared

  • Similarities: both are Muslim-majority countries; both remained under British rule until 1947 (Bangladesh was part of Pakistan until 1971); agriculture is important in both; bread/rice is the common food.
  • Differences: the national language of Pakistan is Urdu and of Bangladesh is Bengali; Pakistan has the Indus plain and mountains, Bangladesh has the Brahmaputra/Ganga delta and heavy rainfall.

How Landforms Affect Lifestyle

  • In mountain regions, people rear livestock and live in wooden houses.
  • In the plains, there is agriculture and trade, and a dense population lives there.
  • On islands (Maldives), there is fishing.
  • In coastal regions, ports and trade provide employment.

Important Professions

Agriculture (farming), fishing, livestock rearing, textile industry, handicrafts, trade, jobs (teacher, doctor, engineer), labour and service work.

mcqs.why: Both are Muslim-majority countries, both remained under British rule until 1947 (Bangladesh was part of Pakistan until 1971), and agriculture and bread/rice food are common in both.

options: rear livestock and live in wooden houses
mcqs.why: The book says landforms affect lifestyle: in mountain regions people rear livestock and live in wooden houses; in plains there is agriculture, trade and dense population; on islands there is fishing.

mcqs.why: The important professions listed are agriculture (farming), fishing, livestock rearing, textile industry, handicrafts, trade, jobs, labour and service work.

lessons.title: People and Their Work
lessons.notes_html:
Four Stages of Economic Activities

StageMeaningExamples
Primary activitiesActivities which use land resources directly, such as land, water and mineralsAgriculture, fishing, mining, forestry
Secondary activitiesActivities which use raw material to make new thingsTextile industry, sugar industry
Tertiary (third-stage) activitiesActivities which provide servicesTrade, transport, banking, education, health
Fourth-stage activitiesInformation and decision-making servicesResearch, planning, management, computer and IT services

Workers of the Fourth Stage and Their Skills

  • Scientist/researcher — skill of research and experiments.
  • Planner — skill of planning and analysis.
  • Manager/administrator — skill of management and decision-making.
  • Computer programmer — skill of computers and software.
  • Teacher/professor — skill of teaching and giving information.
  • Doctor/medical expert — skill of treatment and research.

Workers and the Skills They Need

WorkerSkills needed
BankingAccounting, money management, dealing with customers
FarmingKnowledge of land, seed, water and weather
Machine-makingSkill of operating and repairing machines
FishingSailing a boat, catching fish and knowledge of weather
BusinessmanSkill of buying and selling, accounting and negotiation
TeacherSkill of teaching, explaining and discipline
Coach (guide)Giving training and knowledge of the game
CleaningKnowledge of cleanliness and health principles

Cost of Taking Food to the Market

The cost of taking fruits and vegetables from the field to the local market includes transport, labour, packing and market fees. Whether food prices are within a family's reach is judged by keeping household expenditure, market prices, income and seasonal prices in view. Job advertisements in newspapers show the nature of work, salary, working hours and the skills required.

mcqs.q: The activities which use land resources such as land, water and minerals are called ____ activities.
mcqs.why: Primary activities are obtained directly from land resources — agriculture, fishing, mining and forestry. Secondary activities make new things from raw material.

mcqs.q: ____ activities use raw material to make new things.
mcqs.why: Secondary activities use raw material to make new things; the textile industry and sugar industry are its examples. Tertiary activities provide services instead of goods.

mcqs.why: Tertiary (third-stage) activities provide services — trade, transport, banking, education and health. Fourth-stage activities provide information and decision-making services.

mcqs.why: Fourth-stage activities are information and decision-making services: research, planning, management, and computer and IT services.

mcqs.why: The book's list of fourth-stage workers says the computer programmer uses the skill of computers and software. A scientist uses research and experiments; a manager uses management and decision-making.

options: Accounting, money management and dealing with customers
mcqs.why: The T-chart says banking needs accounting, money management and dealing with customers. Farming needs knowledge of land, seed, water and weather.

mcqs.why: The T-chart lists for fishing: sailing a boat, catching fish and knowledge of weather. Weather knowledge keeps the fisherman safe and helps him find fish.

mcqs.why: Making new things from raw material is a secondary activity; the textile industry (cloth from cotton) and the sugar industry are the book's examples.

mcqs.why: The book's activity says to ask a farmer or trader about the cost in transport, labour, packing and market fees of taking produce from the field to the market.

mcqs.why: The fourth-stage workers list includes the teacher/professor, whose skill is teaching and giving information. The doctor at this stage uses the skill of treatment and research.

lessons.notes_html:
Identify the Landform

DescriptionLandform
A low-lying piece of low landPlain
A depression between two plateaus (or mountains)Valley
A landform with a wide base, steep slope and pointed peakMountain
A high and flat place, formed as the product of a plain (by erosion/deposition)Plateau

Importance of Mountains

  1. Rivers rise from mountains and give water for farming and drinking.
  2. Mountains are a treasure of forests, wildlife and minerals.
  3. Mountains are places of tourism and recreation.
  4. Mountains form the natural borders of countries.
  5. Wood, herbs and minerals are obtained from mountains.

How Mountains Are Formed — Three Ways

(1) Fold mountains — the layers of rock bend when plates collide. (2) Dome mountains — through the uplift of the land and magma rising up. (3) Volcanic mountains — through lava erupting and hardening.

How People Use Mountains

  • Forest production — obtaining wood, herbs and plants.
  • Extracting minerals — taking minerals from mines.
  • Farming — growing tea and fruits on mountain slopes.
  • Recreation — excursions, snowfall and tourism in the mountains.

Types of Industries and Their Difference

TypeWorkExamples
Primary industriesGive natural resources directly from landAgriculture, fishing, mining
Secondary industriesMake goods from raw materialCloth, sugar, steel
Third-stage servicesProvide servicesTrade, banking, transport
Fourth-stage servicesProvide information and decisionsResearch, management, IT

Places for these stages in South Asia: primary — fields, mines, forests; secondary — factories, mills; tertiary — markets, banks, schools, hospitals; fourth-stage — universities, research institutions, IT companies. The activities of South Asia's inhabitants include religions (Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, Christianity), social life (language, dress, food), politics (democracy, monarchy) and the economy (agriculture, industry, trade).

Basic Features to Show on the Map

The Karakoram mountain range, the Deccan Plateau, the Balochistan Plateau, the coastal plains of Sri Lanka, the Himalaya and the Indus plains in Pakistan.

Why Peace Is Necessary in South Asia

Peace increases trade, education and progress; people learn from one another's culture and the inhabitants of all countries live in prosperity. War and quarrels increase poverty, unemployment and destruction. Therefore all countries should work together for peace.

lessons.title: Population
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Population?

Population means the number of people living in a town, city or village. If many people live together in a place, the population of that place is high; if few live there, the population is low.

Population Density

Population density means the number of people living in one unit of an area. If many people live together in an area, the population of that area is dense; if few live there, the population is sparse.

Why Do People Live in a Particular Region?

  1. Availability of fertile land and water.
  2. Employment opportunities (factories, trade, jobs).
  3. Education and health facilities.

According to the book's 2015 table, the largest population in the world was China's, followed by India's. Experts say that by 2050 the total population of the world will become 9.6 billion; more children being born and a fall in the death rate are its reasons.

Migration

People migrate (move) from an area for common reasons: employment, education, shortage of water, political disputes or better facilities. Pakistan's population is divided among its provinces — Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan and others — which can be shown on a pie graph.

lessons.title: Growing Population of South Asia
lessons.notes_html:
Reasons for the Increase in Population in Pakistan

  1. The birth rate is higher than the death rate.
  2. Better health facilities and a fall in the death rate.
  3. Early-age marriage.
  4. The desire for more children.
  5. Little awareness about family planning.
  6. Poverty and considering children a source of income.

Population Trends in South Asia

  • The population is continuously increasing because the birth rate is higher than the death rate.
  • Most people live in plain and fertile regions.
  • Migration towards cities is increasing.
  • Pakistan, India and Bangladesh are among the most populous countries of the world.

Why Has the Death Rate Fallen in the World?

There has been a dramatic fall in the death rate because health facilities have improved, treatment and vaccines for diseases are available, cleanliness has improved, availability of food has increased, and child deaths have decreased.

More Men Than Women in Pakistan

According to the book there are more men than women in Pakistan. Its common reasons are considered to be: giving more importance to boys, fewer health facilities for women, and less care of girls.

Controlling the Increase — Letter to the Editor

To control the increase in population, the government should spread education, give health facilities, create awareness about family planning, focus on women's education and increase employment opportunities. Educating the public is one way of controlling the increase in population — the poster message is: "Education is the best way to control population."

China's One-Child Policy

The population in China had increased very much, so the government adopted a one-child policy so that the increase in population could be controlled.

lessons.title: Growing Population — Problems and Solutions
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Overpopulation?

Overpopulation means the number of people which is more than the resources of a place — people increase so much that it becomes difficult to maintain a reasonable standard of living for them.

Problems Arising Because of Overpopulation

  • Shortage of housing facilities — people do not get houses to live in and dirt increases in densely populated areas.
  • Pressure on health facilities — patients increase in hospitals and not everyone gets treatment.
  • Shortage of water — more people need more water for drinking and farming, but water decreases.
  • Unemployment — jobs are few and job-seekers are many.

Standard of Living

Housing facility, food, water, education and health care affect the standard of living of the people of South Asia: where these facilities are few, the standard of living is low; where facilities are more, the standard is better.

Why Does Population Migrate?

Employment, education, shortage of water and land, natural disasters, political disputes and the search for better facilities.

Suggestions to the Government for Controlling Population

Spread education; give health facilities; create awareness of family planning; increase women's education; increase employment opportunities; and enforce the law on the age of child marriage. The awareness banner says: "The rapid increase in population is an obstacle in fulfilling basic needs (food, water, house, school, job)" — and shows the benefits of a small family.

If the Pupils in Your Classroom Doubled

  • Sitting space will decrease.
  • The teacher will be able to give less time to each pupil.
  • Books, copies and material will fall short.
  • Noise and dirt will increase.
  • Cleanliness and air will decrease.
  • Not everyone will get equal attention.

Why Are Some Regions Sparsely Populated?

Sparsely populated regions are sparse because water, fertile land, employment and facilities are few there; the climate is harsh (deserts, snowy regions, mountains); or the land is not suitable for farming.

mcqs.q: Overpopulation means ____.
options: a high birth rate in one year
the number of people being more than the resources of a place

Distribution and Density of Population

Distribution of population means how people are spread over an area — many in some places, few in others. Density of population means the number of people living in one unit of an area. Distribution tells the spread; density tells the number per unit.

Why Are There More Children in Developing Countries?

  • The birth rate is high.
  • Marriage takes place at an early age.
  • There is a desire for more children.
  • There is little awareness about family planning.

Why Are There Fewer Children in Developed Countries?

  • Education is greater.
  • Marriage takes place late.
  • Family planning is common.
  • People prefer a small family.

Why Do People in South Asia Want More Children?

People in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh want more children because children are considered a source of income and support in old age, marriage takes place at an early age, there is little awareness about education and family planning, and in some families boys are given more importance.

Reasons for Unequal Distribution of Population in the World

Availability of water and fertile land, climate, employment opportunities, education and health facilities and transport. Where these facilities exist the population is dense; where they do not exist it is sparse.

Factors Affecting Population Density (concept map)

  • Raw material for factories — where raw material exists there are factories and employment, and population becomes dense.
  • Less fertile soil — where soil is less fertile there is less farming, and population remains sparse.
  • Employment opportunities — where there is employment, people come and live.
  • Availability of water; climate; education and health facilities; transport.

Map of Population Density in South Asia

Colour the densely populated parts — the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra plains and coastal regions — in red, and the sparsely populated parts — mountains, deserts and dense forests — in yellow. A bar graph of the school can be made by writing the names of the classes on one axis and the number of pupils on the other axis.

lessons.title: Why Do We Make Choices
lessons.notes_html:
Scarcity

Our wants are unlimited and our resources are limited. Scarcity is a situation in which all the things and services which people need are not available. Scarcity occurs because our wants are unlimited but resources (time, money, goods) are limited. People cannot obtain all the things and services which they need, therefore they have to make a choice.

Choice

Choice means selecting one out of several alternatives. We have to make choices because resources are limited and we cannot fulfil all wants at one time. Choice is actually a decision in which we use our time, money and abilities.

Factors We Keep in Mind When Making a Choice

  • Income — how much money we have.
  • Cost — what is the price of the thing.
  • Wants — how much we need it.
  • Values — which things we give importance to in our life.

Values

Values are the things to which we give importance in our life, such as honesty, truthfulness, hospitality, education and family. Values affect our choices because we choose those things which match our values; for example, a person who gives importance to education will spend money on books. That is why every child spends fifty rupees of Eidi on different things — every child's wants, likes and values are different.

Wants and How They Are Fulfilled

WantMeans of fulfilling it
ShoesBuying from a shoe shop
Horse ridingAt a horse-riding club or recreational place
Watching a filmAt the cinema or on TV
Eating fish and chipsFrom a restaurant or shop
Opening a bank accountIn a bank

Examples of Choice in Daily Life

  • Asif's two gifts: he can take only one of the two gifts he likes; the other gift which he gives up is his opportunity cost.
  • The blocks area: when many pupils want to use an area where only four can play at one time, the solution is a turn system — give each pupil a fixed time (such as 15 minutes) and put up a turn list.
  • The pencils: pencils were fewer than the number of pupils (scarcity), so when the pencils finished, the remaining pupils got no pencil despite having money.
  • Gift shopping: Anil's father got the toy car because it was available (availability); Shahid's father had to buy a scooter because the bike had finished in the store (scarcity/availability); Tariq's father could not buy the toy car because he did not have suitable money (income/cost).

mcqs.why: Scarcity means all the things and services which people need are not available, because wants are unlimited while resources are limited.

mcqs.why: Choice means selecting one out of several alternatives. It is a decision in which we use our time, money and abilities, because we cannot fulfil all wants at one time.

lessons.title: Competition and Compromise (Movie Game)
lessons.notes_html:
Trade-Off

We have to make choices because we face scarcity. The process of choosing with limited resources and time is called making a trade-off. When we give up one thing to obtain another thing, it is called a trade-off.

Cost and Benefit

  • Cost: whatever has to be given (money, time or another thing) to obtain something is its cost.
  • Benefit: the profit or advantage obtained from something is its benefit.

Production Possibility Frontier (PPF)

A graph which shows the trade-off in decision-making for facing scarcity is called the Production Possibility Frontier (PPF).

Spending One Hundred Rupees — Four Possible Ways

OptionHow the 100 rupees are spent
1Shoes 100; everything else 0
2Clothes 50, Food 30, Film 20
3Food 40, Gift to friends 30, Gift for family 30
4Gift for family 50, Saving 50

You may spend all the money on one thing, some on one thing and some on another, and you may also save some of it — saving all is also in your control.

Factors (Apart from Capital) Which Affect Our Choice

  1. Time.
  2. Wants and desires.
  3. Values.
  4. Availability (whether the thing is available or not).
  5. Likes and interests.
  6. Pressure/advice of family and friends.
  7. Weather and occasion.

Future Consequences of Choices

  • Abid starts smoking at eighteen: health will deteriorate, money will be wasted, and study and future will be badly affected.
  • Zoya leaves school at eleven: education will remain incomplete, a good job will not be found, and earnings in the future will be low.
  • Shahid leaves school at ten and works in a garage: he will remain deprived of education, will do low-wage work, and chances of progress will decrease.

mcqs.why: Making a trade-off means choosing with limited resources and time: when we give up one thing to obtain another thing, it is called a trade-off.

mcqs.why: The Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) is the graph which shows the trade-offs in decision-making when facing scarcity — the possible combinations of two things that can be obtained.

options: whatever has to be given (money, time or another thing) to obtain something
mcqs.why: Cost is whatever has to be given — money, time or another thing — to obtain something. Benefit, in contrast, is the profit or advantage obtained from something.
