options: the profit or advantage obtained from something
mcqs.why: Benefit is the profit or advantage obtained from something. A good choice is one whose benefit is greater than its cost.

mcqs.why: The factors listed are time, wants and desires, values, availability, likes and interests, pressure/advice of family and friends, and weather and occasion.

options: She will get a good job quickly

lessons.title: Opportunity Cost
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Opportunity Cost?

Opportunity cost is the price of that second-best alternative which could have been chosen but was not chosen — the thing which has to be given up to obtain something is its opportunity cost. Every economic decision has some opportunity cost because resources are limited: when we choose one thing, we have to give up another.

If there is no opportunity cost of spending something, we call it free — such as the air for breathing.

Consumers and Producers

  • Consumers — those people who use goods and services to fulfil their personal needs and wants.
  • Producers — individuals and institutions which use their resources in the production of goods and services.

Examples of Choices and Their Opportunity Costs

Who is choosing?What is chosen?Opportunity cost (given up)
Waqas (individual)New computer for his officeNew fax machine
Asifa (individual)A lollipop from the school canteenTen-rupee chocolates
Minister (government)Building a new highwayBenefiting the unemployed
Abid (individual)New sweaterThe shoes he saw in the store
A company (business)A new machine for goodsRecruiting new workers
A family (household)Spending on repairing broken healthSeaside recreation
A country (government)Buying weaponsMaking weapons

How the Government Faces Opportunity Costs

The government's budget is limited. When the government spends money on one work (such as building a highway), it has to give up another work (such as helping the unemployed), and the given-up work is the opportunity cost of that spending.

Everyday Situations

  • With 25 rupees: buying a candy bar (choice) — saving the money in the money box (opportunity cost).
  • With 30 minutes: playing cricket (choice) — watching TV (opportunity cost).
  • Choosing cricket coaching — swimming lessons are the opportunity cost.
  • Showing a film to friends at a beach party — feeding them outside is the opportunity cost.
  • Donating for school sports equipment — keeping the money for oneself is the opportunity cost.

options: the price of the second-best alternative which could have been chosen
mcqs.why: Opportunity cost is the price of that second-best alternative which could have been chosen but was not chosen — the thing given up to obtain something.

mcqs.why: The book says if there is no opportunity cost of spending something, we call it free — such as the air for breathing, which we do not have to give up anything to use.

mcqs.why: Consumers use goods and services to fulfil their personal needs and wants. Producers are the individuals and institutions which use resources to produce goods and services.

mcqs.why: Producers use their resources in the production of goods and services. The minister, a company, Waqas and Asifa in the table are examples of choosers — individuals, government and business.

mcqs.why: The table lists the company (business) choosing a new machine; recruiting new workers is what it had to give up — the opportunity cost.

options: resources are limited, and choosing one thing means giving up another
mcqs.why: The book explains that every economic decision has an opportunity cost because resources are limited; when we choose one thing we have to give up another, and the given-up thing is the opportunity cost.

mcqs.q: A family gives up seaside recreation to spend that money on repairing broken health. The opportunity cost is ____.
mcqs.why: The family chose to spend on health; the seaside recreation it gave up is the opportunity cost of that decision.

mcqs.why: In the model table for this situation, buying the candy bar is the choice (because the pupil likes sweets) and saving the money is the opportunity cost — the alternative given up.

chapters.title: Unit 8: Production of Goods and Services

lessons.title: What Goods and Services Are Produced
lessons.notes_html:
Goods and Services

  • Goods — the things which we buy to fulfil our needs and wishes, which we can see, feel and touch. Examples: food items, furniture, electronic goods.
  • Services — the work or process which we buy to fulfil our needs and wishes. Examples: hairdressing service, a doctor's medical service.

Whether goods and services are government or private is decided by whether they are sold and at what price.

Private and Government Goods and Services

TypeDefinitionExamples
Private goods and servicesGoods and services produced in the private sector, provided to consumers at a priceA book bought from a shop, private school education
Government goods and servicesThe goods and services which the government provides free for the betterment of society, available to everyone free or at a very low priceRoads, parks, government schools, hospitals, police
Merit goodsGoods whose benefits reach other people too, not only the userVaccination (from the exercise)
Consumer goodsThe things which consumers buy and usePencils, books, toys
Capital goodsThe things which are used to produce more goods and servicesBuildings, machines, a truck used for transporting goods

Producers are the people who produce goods and provide services — for example a craftsman, a shopkeeper, a factory.

Consumer Goods and Capital Goods

Consumer goods are bought and used by consumers, such as pencils, books and toys. Capital goods are used to produce other goods and services, such as buildings, machines and a truck (when it is used for transporting goods).

How the Government Takes Part in Public Welfare

The government provides public welfare goods and services — schools, libraries, police, hospitals, the communication network, street lights and national defence — which are available to everyone free or at a very low price, because they are used collectively. The government also provides services like hospitals free or at a very low price for public welfare. The benefits of vaccination reach not only the person vaccinated but other people too.

Private Goods Are Bought at a Price

Consumers buy private goods and services and pay their price, whereas government goods are available to everyone free or at a very low price. In your neighbourhood, government goods and services include the government school, park, road, street light, hospital, police station and library; the government gives education in government schools, treatment in hospitals and drinking water free or at a low price.

mcqs.why: Capital goods are used to produce other goods and services, such as buildings, machines and a truck used for transporting goods. Consumer goods, like pencils and toys, are bought and used by consumers.

mcqs.why: Consumer goods are the things which consumers buy and use — pencils, books and toys. A school building or a bus is a capital good because it is used to provide a service.

mcqs.q: Vaccination is given in the exercise as an example of a merit good because ____.
options: its benefits reach other people too, not only the person vaccinated
mcqs.why: The chapter's table notes that vaccination is the exercise's example of a merit good, whose benefits reach other people too. The government provides such services for public welfare.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a government good or service?
options: A book bought from a shop
A shirt bought at a price
mcqs.why: Government goods and services — roads, parks, government schools, hospitals, police — are available to everyone free or at a very low price. A bought book and private school education are private.

mcqs.q: Producers are ____.
options: the people who produce goods and provide services
mcqs.why: The book defines producers as the people who produce goods and provide services — for example a craftsman, a shopkeeper or a factory.

mcqs.q: Why are government welfare goods available to everyone free or at a very low price?
options: Because they are of low quality by law
Because shops refuse to sell them

mcqs.why: A truck, when used for transporting goods, is a capital good because it is used to produce goods and services. Buildings and machines are other examples of capital goods.

lessons.title: Producers of Goods and Services
lessons.notes_html:
Firm and Industry

  • A single business is called a firm. Examples: Peek Freans, Bundu Khan.
  • The group of businesses or producers which provides similar goods and services is called an industry. Examples: the textile industry, the communications industry.
  • A firm is only one part of an industry; an industry is the collective name of many firms producing similar goods and services.

State-Owned Enterprises

The businesses which are owned by the government but are run like private-sector businesses to earn profit are called state-owned enterprises.

Voluntary Organisations

Voluntary organisations are also called non-profit organisations. They feel some need in society and want to fulfil it, without profit.

Types of Producers

TypeDefinitionAimExample
Private-sector producersBusinesses owned by individuals or groups of the private sectorTo earn maximum profitPeek Freans, Bundu Khan
Government-sector producersBusinesses owned by the government; they provide goods and services which the private sector generally does not provide without profitTo meet a public need, not profitGovernment school, hospital, police, roads
Voluntary / non-profit organisationsPrivate organisations based on feeling a need in society and wanting to fulfil itFulfilment of some aim or need, without profitEdhi Foundation

In Your Neighbourhood

Private businesses give shop goods, a barber's service and private school education at a price. The government provides the government school, hospital, park, road and police. A voluntary organisation can be formed in a school to meet a real need — such as cleanliness, shortage of books or help for poor pupils — without profit.

mcqs.why: An industry is the collective name of many firms producing similar goods and services — for example the textile industry and the communications industry. A firm is only one part of it.

mcqs.why: They are single businesses, so they are firms. The textile industry and communications industry, being groups of many firms, are industries.

lessons.title: Productivity and Producers' Goals
lessons.notes_html:
Two Kinds of Tax

  • Income tax — a tax which is paid on the amount which is the income of a person or a business.
  • Sales tax — the tax which is collected along with the price of a good or service.

Factors of Production

FactorMeaningExamplesIncome
LandNature's gift; all natural resources used to prepare goods and servicesFarm land, coalRent
LabourThe human effort which prepares goods and services; the physical and mental abilities of workersA farmer's physical labour, a doctor's mental labourWages
CapitalThe financial resources, tools, machines, furniture and buildings used to run a businessFactory machines, the shop buildingProfit
EnterpriseThe person who organises labour, capital and land, takes decisions and faces the risks of businessA shopkeeper running a shop, an industrialist setting up a factoryProfit

A person who comes into the field with new ideas, takes decisions and bears their consequences is called an entrepreneur (businessman).

Interdependence and Specialisation

  • Interdependence: consumers and producers depending on each other — consumers buy goods from producers, and producers depend on consumers' buying.
  • Specialisation: when some people concentrate in their production on some particular goods and services — for example, one person makes only shoes; one factory makes only soap.

Aims of Private-Sector Producers

Commercial aims: making profit; being one's own boss; providing a good or service which can be sold; the social status obtained from one's business. The aims of some private producers can also be non-commercial: they want to meet some need visible in society; their aim is not to earn profit but only to cover expenses. Such businesses are called non-profit or voluntary organisations, like the Edhi Foundation.

Interviewing a Producer

For example, a shopkeeper: sells shop goods; works about 60 hours a week; training is the experience of shopkeeping; income is some thousand rupees per month; good points — own boss, contact with customers; bad points — long hours, little holiday.

Why Does the Government Provide Some Goods and Services?

  • To provide a good service which the private sector cannot give because of profit.
  • Providing these goods and services is more expensive; their importance is far greater than the price the consumer pays.
  • This promotes social harmony, justice and equality because they are equally available to all.
  • They are also called collective goods or services, from which very many people benefit; if the private sector produced them, it would not be possible to provide them to all.

How Does the Government Pay for These?

The government pays from taxes and fees. It collects taxes from people and businesses — income tax and sales tax — and uses that same money in the preparation of services. Sometimes a fee is also collected, such as the fee for passing through highway toll posts or for recreation in a public park.

Circular Flow — Interdependence in the Economy

Householders (families) give the factors of production (land, labour, capital) to the producers and in return receive rent, wages and profit. The producers make goods and services from these factors; householders buy those goods and services and the money goes back to the producers. In this way consumers and producers depend on each other.

mcqs.q: A tax which is paid on the income of a person or a business is called ____.

mcqs.why: Sales tax is collected along with the price of a good or service — when you buy a thing from a shop, its price includes this tax, which reaches the government.

mcqs.q: A person who comes into the field with new ideas, takes decisions and bears their consequences is called an ____.
mcqs.why: An entrepreneur organises land, labour and capital, takes decisions and faces the risks coming in business — for example a shopkeeper running a shop or an industrialist setting up a factory.

mcqs.q: Land, as a factor of production, means ____ and its income is rent.
options: nature's gift — all natural resources used to prepare goods and services
mcqs.why: Land is nature's gift: all the natural resources used to prepare goods and services, such as farm land and coal. Its income is called rent, while the income of labour is wages.

mcqs.q: Labour means the human effort which prepares goods and services, and its income is called ____.
mcqs.why: Labour is the physical and mental abilities of workers — a farmer's physical labour, a doctor's mental labour. The income of labour is wages.

mcqs.q: Capital includes ____ used to run a business.
options: financial resources, tools, machines, furniture and buildings
mcqs.why: Capital is the financial resources, tools, machines, furniture and buildings which are used to run a business — for example factory machines and the shop building.

mcqs.q: Specialisation means ____.
options: some people concentrating on producing some particular goods and services
mcqs.why: Specialisation is when some people concentrate in their production on particular goods and services — one person makes only shoes; one factory makes only soap.

mcqs.q: Interdependence means ____.
options: consumers and producers depending on each other
mcqs.why: Interdependence is consumers and producers depending on each other: consumers buy goods from producers, and producers depend on consumers' buying. The circular flow diagram shows this.

mcqs.q: Which is a commercial aim of private-sector producers?
options: Making profit and being one's own boss
mcqs.why: Commercial aims are making profit, being one's own boss, providing a good or service which can be sold, and the social status obtained from business. Non-commercial aims belong to non-profit organisations.

mcqs.q: How does the government pay for the goods and services provided to the people?
options: From taxes and fees collected from people and businesses
From the income of one shop
mcqs.why: The government collects taxes (income tax and sales tax) and sometimes fees — such as highway toll posts or park entry — and uses that same money to prepare the services for the people.

mcqs.q: Goods and services provided by the government to all are also called ____ goods or services.
mcqs.why: They are called collective goods or services because very many people benefit from them; they promote social harmony, justice and equality as they are equally available to all.

mcqs.q: In the circular flow, householders give the factors of production to producers and in return receive ____.
mcqs.why: Householders (families) give land, labour and capital to producers and receive rent, wages and profit in return; then they buy the goods and services producers make, and the money flows back to the producers.

Difference of Aims

  • Private business enterprises — aim: to earn maximum profit (examples: Peek Freans, Bundu Khan).
  • Non-governmental organisations — aim: to meet some need without profit (example: Edhi Foundation).
  • State-owned enterprises — owned by the government but run like the private sector for profit.

When a Family Cannot Pay

If a family cannot pay the fee for sending its children to school, the children can study in a government school free or at a low fee. If a family has no money for its children's treatment, treatment can be obtained from a government hospital free or at a low price. The solution in both situations lies in the government's public services.

Debate of the Three Producers

  • The private producer says: "I earn profit by selling goods."
  • The government producer says: "I give services to all free or at a low price, such as schools and hospitals."
  • The non-profit producer says: "I meet some need without profit."

Together the three provide goods and services in the economy. Government services — schools, hospitals, roads and parks — are available to all free or at a low price and benefit everyone. Services can also be done for the old people of the neighbourhood: spend time with them, help them in shopping, or read a story to them, regularly.

chapters.title: Unit 9: The Individual, Community and Group in South Asia

lessons.title: Individuals in South Asian Societies
lessons.notes_html:
Important Facts

  • In Bhutan the Dzongkha language is spoken (its national language).
  • The special festival of Nepal is Dashain.
  • The most followed religions in South Asia are Hinduism and Islam — the chapter's table lists both these religions in many countries.

Community

A community is a social unit whose values are the same or which is situated in one geographical area (a village or a town).

Identity

Identity is the set of characteristics which give a person a distinct recognition from others. It is formed by factors such as family, culture, food, festivals, lifestyle, games and media. The family is the most important factor in forming identity: its role is the care of children, education, guidance and protection.

Culture

Culture is the collection of the living ways, values, customs, language, food, festivals, fairs and arts of a group or society.

How the Countries of South Asia Differ

  • Languages: Urdu, Punjabi, Sindhi in Pakistan; Dzongkha in Bhutan — every country has its own languages.
  • Religions: Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Christianity.
  • Festivals: Eid-ul-Fitr, Eid-ul-Azha, Diwali, Dashain, Nowruz, Christmas, Easter, Jashn-e-Afghan.
  • Customs and national characteristics differ from country to country.

Common Beliefs and Values

The common beliefs and values of the people of South Asia include: belief in God, visiting places of worship, respect for elders and good behaviour, and decisions of the head of the family.

Modern and Traditional Lifestyles

South Asia is becoming a modern region, but a traditional lifestyle still exists here. Traditional lifestyle: traditional foods, festivals, customs and the family system. Modern lifestyle: media, technology, new foods and new ways. Both still exist together today.

mcqs.why: The book says Dzongkha is spoken in Bhutan; it is Bhutan's national language. Languages differ from country to country in South Asia — Urdu, Punjabi and Sindhi are spoken in Pakistan.

mcqs.why: The special festival of Nepal is Dashain. Other famous festivals of the region are Eid-ul-Fitr, Eid-ul-Azha, Diwali, Nowruz, Christmas, Easter and Jashn-e-Afghan.

options: the set of characteristics which give a person a distinct recognition from others
mcqs.why: Identity is formed by factors such as family, culture, food, festivals, lifestyle, games and media, and it gives a person distinct recognition from others.

options: living ways, values, customs, language, food, festivals, fairs and arts

mcqs.why: The family is the most important factor in forming identity; its role is the care of children, education, guidance and protection. Culture, food, festivals, lifestyle, games and media also contribute.

options: Respect for elders and good behaviour

mcqs.why: The modern lifestyle includes media, technology, new foods and new ways, while the traditional lifestyle includes traditional foods, festivals, customs and the family system. Both exist together in South Asia today.

mcqs.why: The festivals collage lists Eid-ul-Fitr, Eid-ul-Azha, Diwali, Dashain, Nowruz, Christmas, Easter and Jashn-e-Afghan as the important festivals of South Asia.

lessons.title: The Individual's Relation with the Group in South Asian Countries
lessons.notes_html:
Social Group

A social group is a collection of two or more individuals which has some particular characteristics and whose values and standards show similarity. Examples: a cricket team, class pupils.

Primary Group

Primary groups are groups which are very close to one another. They are traditionally few in number and long-lasting, and their members feel a personal connection with their group. Examples: the family and close friends.

Secondary Group

Secondary groups are another type of social group. They can be large and small but are mostly separate and of short duration. They are generally found at workplaces or in schools. Examples: the class and the games team (also office workers).

PointPrimary GroupSecondary Group
ClosenessVery close to one anotherMostly separate
NumberFew in numberCan be large or small
DurationLong-lastingOf short duration
ConnectionMembers feel a personal connectionFormed for work or study purposes
ExamplesFamily, close friendsClass, games team, office workers

Social Roles

  • Parents — care of children, education, guidance, protection.
  • Children — going to school, respecting everyone, good behaviour, relations with companions.
  • The teacher, pupil, doctor etc. each have their own roles.

Groups We Belong To

Primary groups: family, close friends. Secondary groups: class, games team, social network groups. In a group of friends, each member has a status (position) and a role is expected of him — such as helping one another, respect and working together. The famous groups of South Asia include the family, class, cricket team, group of friends and office workers.

options: A games team for one match

lessons.title: Unit 9 — End Exercises
lessons.notes_html:
Quick Facts

  • Dashain is the famous festival of Nepal.
  • The languages Pashto and Dari are spoken in Afghanistan.
  • The social status of an individual in a group is called his status.
  • Members have individual and collective rights in a group.

Aspects of the Identity of the People of South Asia

The factors forming identity are: family, culture, lifestyle, food, media, technology and festivals; besides these, language, religion, customs, fairs and national characteristics are also aspects of identity.

Role and Responsibilities of a Member of a Social Group

Every member has a status (position) in the group and a role, which is the action expected of him in that position. Example: parents have a status, and their role is care of children, education, guidance and protection; children are expected to go to school, respect everyone, behave well and develop relations with companions.

Why Do People Join a Social Group?

  • They value connection and acceptance.
  • Belonging to a group increases a person's sense of belonging.
  • It gives a feeling of moral support.
  • It can give guidance in life.
  • It helps in understanding connection and role.
  • Being wanted gives meaning to life.

Primary and Secondary Groups in Pakistan's Provinces

Similarity: in every province, primary groups (family, close friends) and secondary groups (class, team, office) are found, and all have common characteristics, values and roles. Difference: primary groups are close, few and long-lasting; secondary groups are separate and of short duration; languages, foods, festivals and customs differ between provinces.

Common Points for Discussion

Similarities among the people of South Asia: common beliefs, values and the family system. Customs: respect for elders and hospitality. Festivals: Eids, Diwali, Dashain and Nowruz. A pictorial scenario about the countries of South Asia (SAARC) is made from the chapter's facts: the eight countries of South Asia, their shared cultures, festivals, languages and religions, and the idea of mutual cooperation; the values for such cooperation are respect for one another, cooperation, protection of shared culture and festivals, and equality of all countries. The lifestyle pictures of South Asian countries show their foods, clothes, festivals, houses and games.

mcqs.why: The social position of an individual in a group is called his status, while the action expected of him in that position is his role. Parents, for example, have the role of care, education, guidance and protection.

mcqs.q: Members of a group have ____ rights in the group.

options: Family, culture, food, festivals, language and religion

mcqs.why: The factors forming identity are family, culture, lifestyle, food, media, technology and festivals, and also language, religion, customs, fairs and national characteristics.

options: the action expected of him in his position
mcqs.why: Every member has a status (position) in the group and a role — the action expected of him in that position. Children, for example, are expected to go to school and respect everyone.

mcqs.q: Why do people join a social group?
options: They value connection and acceptance; belonging gives a sense of belonging and moral support
Because groups are compulsory by law
mcqs.why: The reasons given are: people value connection and acceptance; belonging increases the sense of belonging; it gives moral support and guidance in life; and being wanted gives meaning to life.

mcqs.q: What is the similarity between the groups of Pakistan's different provinces?
options: All provinces have the same language
In every province primary and secondary groups are found, with common characteristics, values and roles
mcqs.why: In every province primary groups (family, close friends) and secondary groups (class, team, office) are found with common characteristics, values and roles; the differences are that languages, foods, festivals and customs differ between provinces.

mcqs.q: Hospitality and respect for elders are ____ of the people of South Asia.

mcqs.q: The pictorial scenario about South Asian countries is based on the chapter's facts: the eight countries, their shared cultures, festivals, languages and religions, and the idea of ____.
mcqs.why: The scenario uses the chapter's facts — the eight countries of South Asia, shared cultures, festivals, languages and religions — and the idea of mutual cooperation, with values of respect, cooperation and equality of all countries.

lessons.title: Developing Inquiry Skills
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Research (Investigation)?

The process of investigation is like detective work. It includes asking a key question, collecting information or evidence, analysing it and drawing a conclusion from it. It has four steps: asking a question, collecting information, analysing information, presenting information.

The Four Steps of Research

StepWorkExample (keeping our society clean and green)
1. Make some research questionPrepare a list of possible questionsHow can we keep our society clean and green?
2. Collecting informationCollect information from different sources (books, newspapers, survey, internet)Collect information about cleanliness from books and a survey
3. Analysing informationLook at the information obtained and think about the answer to the research question from itDraw the conclusion from the collected information why cleanliness is necessary
4. Presenting informationPresent the collected information through a paragraph/graph/posterWrite a paragraph on cleanliness or make a bar graph

Ten Sources of Information

Books; newspapers; internet; TV; radio; talking to teachers/experts; survey; museum; artefacts/works of art; autobiographies/traditional tales.

Presenting Information

  • Oral: speech, discussion, telling a story.
  • Written: writing a paragraph, essay, report.
  • Pictorial graph: making a bar graph, line graph, poster.

Graphs

In a bar graph, the bars (columns) tell the measurement. A change which changes with time can be shown by using a line graph.

Fact and Bias in Inquiry

A statement which can be proved correct is called a fact. Advertisements tell us about the goodness of some product; they are the best example of bias, because they show only one side (the goodness) and ignore the other side.

Comparing Countries

Countries can be compared in three ways: comparing the title, key, compass and scale of maps; comparing the culture, festivals and languages of countries; and comparing location, shape and size on maps.

mcqs.q: The process of investigation is like ____ work.
mcqs.why: Research (investigation) is like detective work: asking a key question, collecting information or evidence, analysing it and drawing a conclusion from it.

mcqs.q: Which is the FIRST step of research?
mcqs.why: The four steps are: 1) make some research question (prepare a list of possible questions), 2) collecting information, 3) analysing information, 4) presenting information.

mcqs.q: In the steps-of-research table, information is collected from different sources such as ____.
mcqs.why: The collecting-information step says to collect information from different sources — books, newspapers, survey, internet. Using several sources makes the research more reliable.

mcqs.q: Analysing information means ____.
options: looking at the information obtained and thinking about the answer to the research question from it
mcqs.why: In the analysis step we look at the collected information and draw the conclusion — for example, concluding from the collected information why cleanliness is necessary.

mcqs.q: Which of these is one of the ten sources of information?
mcqs.why: The ten sources are: books, newspapers, internet, TV, radio, talking to teachers/experts, survey, museum, artefacts/works of art, and autobiographies/traditional tales.

mcqs.q: Speech, discussion and telling a story are ways of presenting information ____.
mcqs.why: The three patterns of presentation are: oral (speech, discussion, telling a story), written (paragraph, essay, report) and pictorial graph (bar graph, line graph, poster).

mcqs.q: In a bar graph, the ____ tell the measurement.
mcqs.why: In a bar graph, the bars (columns) tell the measurement — the taller the bar, the greater the quantity it shows.

mcqs.q: A change which changes with time can be shown by using a ____.
mcqs.why: The book says a change which changes with time can be shown by using a line graph, because the line rises and falls with time.

mcqs.q: Advertisements are the best example of bias because they ____.
options: show only one side (the goodness of the product) and ignore the other side
mcqs.why: Advertisements tell us about the goodness of some product; they show only one side and ignore the other side — that is why they are the best example of bias.

mcqs.q: A statement which can be proved correct is called a ____.
mcqs.why: A statement which can be proved correct is called a fact. In inquiry we must separate facts from opinions and bias.

lessons.title: Developing History Skills
lessons.notes_html:
Historians Are Like Detectives

Historians are like detectives — they ask countless questions about the past: What happened? When? Where? How? Why? They collect evidence and study primary and secondary sources. History is the study of events which happened in the past. We study it because it tells us how many things changed, and it opens our eyes about other cultures.

Primary Sources

A primary source is that part of information about an event/era which was created by a person connected with that event — that is, he was contemporary with the event. Examples: diaries, letters, photographs, buildings, newspapers, cultural exhibits, audio artefacts. Historians research secondary sources through primary sources.

Secondary Sources

A secondary source is one whose creation was not begun by the person who was present in the event (or who was born after the event); it was created by later people and it explains the information obtained from primary sources. Examples: textbook, TV programme, films, games, tales/stories, history books, internet.

PointPrimary SourceSecondary Source
Who made it?A person connected with the event, contemporary with itLater people who were not present in the event
What it doesGives direct information/evidence of the eventExplains the information obtained from primary sources
ExamplesDiaries, letters, photographs, buildings, newspapersTextbook, TV programme, films, history books, internet

The Time Line

An effective way of arranging historical events is the time line. The development of transport, for example, can be shown on a time line in order: from old means (bullock cart, horse) to new means (railway, motor car, aeroplane).

Counting Years: CE and BCE

  • CE (Common Era) — the years after the birth of Jesus Christ are counted.
  • BCE (Before Common Era) — the years before the birth are counted.
  • Examples: Alexander the Great died in 323 BC — that is, 323 years before the birth; Quaid-e-Azam died in 1948 — that is, 1948 years after the birth.
  • One decade is equal to 10 (ten) years.
  • One millennium is equal to 1000 (one thousand) years.

mcqs.q: Historians are like ____ — they ask countless questions about the past.
mcqs.why: Historians are like detectives: they ask questions about the past (What happened? When? Where? How? Why?), collect evidence, and study primary and secondary sources.

mcqs.q: Historians research secondary sources through ____.
mcqs.why: The book says historians research secondary sources through primary sources, because primary sources give the direct evidence from the time of the event.

mcqs.q: An effective way of arranging historical events in order is the ____.
mcqs.why: The time line arranges historical events in the order in which they happened — for example, the development of transport from the bullock cart to the aeroplane.

mcqs.q: One decade is equal to ____ years.
mcqs.why: A decade is a period of ten years. A millennium is a much longer period of one thousand years.

mcqs.q: One millennium is equal to ____ years.
mcqs.why: One millennium is equal to 1000 (one thousand) years. Ten years make one decade and one hundred years make a century.

mcqs.q: A primary source is information about an event which was created by ____.
options: a person born long after the event
a person connected with the event, contemporary with it
mcqs.why: A primary source was created by a person connected with the event — he was contemporary with the event. Diaries, letters, photographs, buildings and newspapers are its examples.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a primary source?
options: A diary written at the time of the event
mcqs.why: Diaries, letters, photographs, buildings, newspapers, cultural exhibits and audio artefacts are primary sources. Textbooks, TV programmes, films and history books are secondary sources.

mcqs.q: A secondary source is one which ____.
options: was created by later people and explains the information obtained from primary sources
mcqs.why: A secondary source was created by later people who were not present in the event, and it explains the information obtained from primary sources — such as a textbook or a history book.

mcqs.q: CE (Common Era) means the years ____ the birth of Jesus Christ.
mcqs.why: CE counts the years after the birth of Jesus Christ, while BCE (Before Common Era) counts the years before the birth. Quaid-e-Azam died in 1948 CE.

mcqs.q: Alexander the Great died in 323 BC, which means ____.
options: 323 years before the birth of Jesus Christ
mcqs.why: The book explains: Alexander the Great died in 323 BC — that is, 323 years before the birth; while 1948 (Quaid-e-Azam's death) is 1948 years after the birth.

mcqs.q: Why do we study history, according to the discussion points?
options: It tells us how many things changed and opens our eyes about other cultures
mcqs.why: We study history because it tells us how many things changed and opens our eyes about other cultures. Historians study it by asking questions and examining evidence.

lessons.title: Developing Geography Skills — Map Making
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Map?

The symbolic presentation of the characteristics of some place, made or presented on a flat surface, is called a map. A map is a symbolic presentation and a shortened reference (a small sketch) of a small surface of the earth.

Four Elements of a Map

ElementHow it helps
TitleTells which place/topic the map is of
Key (symbol)Explains the symbols present on the map — for example, a point shows a city; without the key the map cannot be read
CompassIndicates the north and gives an idea of the correct direction
ScaleTells the relation between the distance on the map and the actual distance on the ground

Two Classifications of Maps

Maps can be divided into general reference maps and thematic maps.

Types of Maps and Their Information

MapInformation it gives
Physical mapThe natural features of an area — river, lake, mountain, plateau, sea, coastal areas, desert
Political mapThe boundaries and provinces of the country
Weather mapThe weather of different parts — high pressure = good weather; low pressure = chances of rain
Topographical mapThe height and shape of the land, shown by contour lines

Topographical Maps and Contour Lines

A topographical map shows the height and shape of a part of the land. It tells height by contour lines: an imaginary line whose all points are of the same height; each line and the distance between shows a difference of ten metres in height. Close lines = sloping land; far lines = flat land; no line = completely flat. Height is also shown by colours and numbers.

Making a Map of Your School

Measure the school ground, building and classroom; choose a scale; and make the map with title, key and compass. Another group can then use your key symbols to correctly identify the rooms of the school building (classroom, office, library, etc.).

mcqs.q: A map is ____.
options: a drawing of one building only
the symbolic presentation of the characteristics of a place on a flat surface
mcqs.why: The book defines a map as the symbolic presentation of the characteristics of some place made on a flat surface — a shortened reference (small sketch) of a small surface of the earth.

mcqs.q: The four elements of a map are title, key, compass and ____.
mcqs.why: The four elements are title, key (symbol), compass and scale. Each one helps in understanding the map in its own way.

mcqs.q: The classifications into which maps can be divided are general reference maps and ____ maps.
mcqs.why: Maps are classified into general reference maps and thematic maps. Physical, political and weather maps give information on particular themes.

mcqs.q: Physical maps show the ____ of an area.
mcqs.why: Physical maps show the natural features of an area — river, lake, mountain, plateau, sea, coastal areas and desert. Political maps show boundaries and provinces.

mcqs.q: Topographical maps show the ____ and ____ of the land.
mcqs.why: Topographical maps show the height and shape of the land, using contour lines, colours and numbers to show height.

mcqs.q: The key (symbol) on a map helps us because ____.
options: it tells the symbols present on the map; without it the map cannot be read
mcqs.why: The key explains the symbols on the map — for example, a point shows a city. To know the symbols it is necessary to understand the key; without it the map cannot be read.

mcqs.q: The scale of a map tells ____.
options: the relation between the distance on the map and the actual distance on the ground
mcqs.why: The scale tells the relation between map distance and actual ground distance. The compass indicates north and direction, and the title tells which place the map is of.

mcqs.q: A contour line is ____.
options: an imaginary line whose all points are of the same height
mcqs.why: A contour line joins points of the same height; each line and the gap between lines shows a difference of ten metres in height. Close lines mean sloping land and far lines mean flat land.

mcqs.q: On a topographical map, close contour lines show ____ land and far lines show ____ land.
mcqs.why: The book says: close lines = sloping land, far lines = flat land, and no line = completely flat land. Height is also shown by colours and numbers.

mcqs.q: On a weather map, low pressure means ____.
mcqs.why: The weather map gives the weather of different parts: high pressure = good weather, low pressure = chances of rain.

mcqs.q: To make a map of your school, after measuring the ground, building and classroom, you should ____.
options: choose a scale and make the map with title, key and compass
mcqs.why: The activity says: measure the school ground, building and classroom; choose a scale; make a map with title, key and compass — then another group can use your key to identify the rooms.

lessons.title: Unit 10 — End Exercises
lessons.notes_html:
Matching: Primary Sources and What They Tell Us

Primary sourceCharacteristics of ancient civilization it tells about
Bones and structuresFood, professions (work)
Building structureBuildings, residence (houses), defence
ShapesReligion, jewellery
Vessels (pots)Food, professions (work)
Tools (implements)Professions (work), defence, transport
Written documentLanguage, education, religion, transport

Note: one primary source can tell about more than one characteristic. The characteristics are: buildings, defence, education, food, residence (houses), jewellery, language, professions (work), religion and transport.

Why Do Historians Examine Primary and Secondary Sources?

For a complete and accurate picture of the past, many sources are needed; primary sources are used for researching secondary sources.

Why Is It Difficult to Know the Truth About the Past?

  • Evidence is incomplete and some evidence is not available.
  • Secondary sources are not proof like primary sources.
  • Writers have their own viewpoint and bias.
  • Fact and opinion must be distinguished.
  • There is no formula for research — it depends on what we want to know and what is available.

Maps — A Suitable Source for Geographers

A map is a symbolic presentation of the characteristics of a place; it presents information in a simple and better way; it shows the size/shape of countries, the locations of features, the difference between places and the distribution of things on the land — and it is from these maps that we begin.

Examining an Unusual Object (investigation)

Examine the object with the steps of investigation: look at its symbols/marks, material and shape. If there is writing on it, it may be an ancient script, and it should be given to an expert (historian/archaeologist); the pattern can tell about the language, art and lifestyle of that era. Artefacts (tools, vessels, jewellery) indicate the goods and technical skill of a culture: they tell what people made, how they lived and how skilled they were. As a historian, base your opinion on the steps of investigation — question, evidence, analysis, conclusion — and keep a distinction between fact and opinion and avoid bias.

Reading the Evidence: A Civilization

  • Source A — remains of animal bones and weapons: the people ate meat, and animal bones and weapons show that they hunted.
  • Source B — vessels for storing grain: they ate grain and would cook food at home/on fire, from the vessels.
  • Source C — pyramids and mountain engravings: they show a religious belief.
  • Opinion from the evidence: this was an organised, religious and skilled civilization.

What We Learned in This Unit

  • Research: asking a question, collecting information, analysing and presenting.
  • Historian's skills: studying primary and secondary sources, measurement of time, sequence and the time line; the study of history is important because it tells how many things changed and opens our eyes about other cultures.
  • Maps: the elements of a map, its types and contour lines. A tourist booklet combines all three: the country's map (title, key, compass, scale), its history (important events, time line) and its geography (physical features, weather).

mcqs.q: In the matching exercise, 'Vessels (pots)' tell us about which characteristics of an ancient civilization?
mcqs.why: Vessels (pots) are matched with food and professions (work). Bones and structures also tell about food and professions, while written documents tell about language, education, religion and transport.

mcqs.q: A 'Written document' as a primary source tells us about ____.
mcqs.why: The matching gives written documents the widest information: language, education, religion and transport. Building structures tell about buildings, residence and defence.

mcqs.q: Tools (implements) tell us about professions, defence and ____.
mcqs.why: Tools (implements) are matched with professions (work), defence and transport. One primary source can tell about more than one characteristic of a civilization.

mcqs.q: Historians examine both primary and secondary sources because ____.
options: a complete and accurate picture of the past needs many sources
mcqs.why: For a complete and accurate picture of the past many sources are needed, and primary sources are used for researching secondary sources.

mcqs.q: Why is it difficult for historians to know the truth about the past?
options: Because evidence is incomplete and some evidence is not available
Because historians do not work hard
Because the past had no events
mcqs.why: The difficulties are: evidence is incomplete and some is unavailable; secondary sources are not proof like primary sources; writers have their own viewpoint and bias; and fact and opinion must be distinguished.

mcqs.q: Maps are a suitable source for geographers because a map ____.
options: is a symbolic presentation of the characteristics of a place and presents information in a simple and better way
mcqs.why: Maps show the size/shape of countries, the locations of features, the difference between places and the distribution of things on the land — and it is from these maps that geographers begin.

mcqs.q: The compass element of a map helps by ____.
options: indicating the north and giving an idea of the correct direction
mcqs.why: The elements help in this way: title tells which place/topic the map is of; key explains the symbols; compass indicates north and direction; scale tells the relation between map distance and actual ground distance.

mcqs.q: If an unusual object has writing on it, it may be an ancient script and it should be given to ____.
mcqs.why: The investigation activity says the object's symbols, material and shape should be examined; if it has writing, it may be an ancient script and should be given to an expert — a historian or archaeologist.

mcqs.q: Artefacts such as tools, vessels and jewellery tell us ____ about a culture.
options: what people made, how they lived and how skilled they were
mcqs.why: Artefacts indicate the goods and technical skill of that culture: they tell what people made, how they lived and how skilled they were.

mcqs.q: Source A (animal bones and weapons) and Source B (vessels for storing grain) show that the people ate ____.
mcqs.why: The evidence reading concludes: people would eat meat (from animal bones) and grain (from vessels); animal bones and weapons show that they hunted, and they would cook food at home/on fire.

mcqs.q: Pyramids and mountain engravings (Source C) show that the civilization had ____.
mcqs.why: Source C shows a religious belief, and the overall opinion from the evidence is that this was an organised, religious and skilled civilization.

mcqs.q: As a historian examining an object, your report should ____.
options: be based on the steps of investigation — question, evidence, analysis, conclusion — keeping fact and opinion separate and avoiding bias
mcqs.why: The activity instructs: base your opinion on the steps of investigation (question, evidence, analysis, conclusion), present the report to the class, keep a distinction between fact and opinion, and avoid bias.

mcqs.q: A tourist booklet of a country should include its map, its history and its ____.
mcqs.why: The booklet combines the three skills of the unit: the country's map (title, key, compass, scale), its history (important events, time line) and its geography (physical features, weather).
